note: Verbatim answers. Scoring is a human step -- see docs/walkthrough-notes.md.

answers.main_question:
That you can ask the same AI the same question in three different ways and get three genuinely different outcomes — one confidently wrong, one that gave up after a huge amount of effort, and one that just looked the answer up and got it right. The lesson I take is that giving a model more room to think is not automatically an improvement, and that the one which 'tried hardest' was the one that failed worst.

The other thing, which took me longer to get but I think is the actual point: the page is grading the AI's working, not just its answers. And then it grades the grader, and tells you the grader is only right about two-thirds of the time when it complains about something.
answers.in_your_own_words: It is a comparison of three ways of asking an AI to solve problems — answer straight away, think it through at length, or let it use tools like a lookup. There are 27 problems, mostly arithmetic and general-knowledge ones, and for each you can open it up and see all three attempts with the AI's full working written out and marked up line by line. There are two extra pages: one saying how reliable the marking is, and one testing whether the AI can be talked out of its answer by someone claiming to know better. It could not be, in any of the 48 attempts.
answers.surprised:
The empty box. Three answers side by side and the middle one just says '— no answer —' after doing 141 steps of work. I did not know that was a thing an AI could do, and seeing it in the middle of the other two made the point immediately, before I had read any of the explanation around it.

I was also surprised by how much the page argues against itself. There is a section literally headed 'What this instrument does not do well', at the top, before the good news. I have not seen anything else presented that way and I found it more persuasive rather than less.
answers.didnt_trust:
Not distrust exactly — more that there are stretches where I cannot tell whether I am being told good news or bad news.

1. 'Classifier agreement with a human — held-out. Cohen's kappa on the sealed set, read once, at a frozen prompt bundle.' I do not know what any of that means. I can see 0.55, and I can see the page says it 'missed its target', so I gather it is worse than hoped — but I could not explain to anyone by how much or why it matters. Same for 'majority-class baseline', 'per-class F1', 'enrichment factor'.

2. '95% CI -0.02 - 1.00'. I do not know what CI is, but even I can see one of those numbers is negative and the other is the maximum, which makes it look like the range covers everything. If that is as bad as it looks, I would want it said in words. If it is not, I would want to know why not.

3. Different parts of the site tell me different things about whether the marking has been checked. One page publishes the checking results. The problem pages say the check has not happened yet. I noticed because the phrase 'not yet measured' appears in a box directly under a percentage, which already felt odd, and then the other page had the numbers. I cannot tell which is current, and it is the thing the whole page says I should care most about.

4. The word 'unsound' is doing a lot of work and I am not sure I have the right idea of it. On one problem the AI got the right answer but a step was marked unsound. So unsound means 'this bit of the working was wrong' rather than 'the answer is wrong'? I think so, but I inferred it rather than being told.

5. I do not know what the problems are testing. Fairhaven, Brightwater and the Meridian Institute do not seem to be real places — so is the AI being asked to look up things that do not exist? If so, that changes what 'wrong' means, and it is never explained.

6. Ten of the 27 are labelled 'planted error' and three are 'illustrative'. So half the list is not real results. I understood that eventually, but at a glance the grid looks like 27 equivalent test results and I nearly took it as one.
answers.would_have_asked:
- In one sentence, is the grading reliable enough to act on or not?
- What does kappa 0.55 mean in plain words — better than a coin flip, or not?
- Which is right: has the marking been checked, or not? Two parts of the site disagree.
- Are Fairhaven and the Meridian Institute made up? If they are, why?
- Does 'unsound step' mean the answer is wrong, or just that part of the working was?
- If I only remember one thing from this page, what should it be?
- Is this about AI in general, or only about this one specific model? The small print mentions a model name I do not recognise, and I cannot tell how far the conclusions travel.
- Can I show this to someone outside the team, and if so what do I tell them it is?
answers.got_stuck:
Twice properly.

On the calibration page, from 'Measured' onwards. The top of that page is in plain English and I followed it. The table underneath is not, and I skimmed it rather than read it, which I suspect is the opposite of what it is for. A one-line plain-language verdict at the top — something like 'the grading currently agrees with a human less often than we want, so treat flags as hints' — would have carried me through the rest.

On the problem grid. Twenty-seven cards where a lot of them are the same problem repeated with different labels. Four identical data-centre questions, three identical garden ones. I assumed at first it was a bug, then worked out the repeats must be variants of some kind, and gave up trying to understand the difference between SE-03, SE-04 and SE-05. I clicked one of the featured links instead, which was the right thing to do and is what the page nudged me toward — but if the featured links had not been there I would probably have stopped at the grid.
